content: In December 2015, a pricing agreement was established between UNITAID, UNAIDS, the Clinton Health Access Initiative, and Aurobindo to introduce dolutegravir (DTG) 50 mg at a cost of $44 per person per year. This initiative aimed to make treatment with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), lamivudine (3TC), and DTG (costing approximately $93–98 per person per year) affordable in lowand middle-income countries covered by the ViiV Healthcare license. The cost of this regimen was designed to be comparable to the TDF + 3TC + efavirenz (EFV) fixed-dose combination. Over time, the cost was expected to decrease further due to the introduction of fixed-dose combinations and increased competition among generic manufacturers of DTG. Additionally, long-term savings were anticipated by reducing the need to switch patients to more expensive second-line regimens. Forecasts from the Clinton Health Access Initiative projected that by the end of 2021, up to 7 million people could be receiving a DTG-containing first-line regimen, as DTG was expected to be provided to new antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiators and some individuals already on non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based ART. For example, South Africa planned to transition up to 4 million people to DTG within two years of its launch. By 2025, widespread adoption of DTG in first-line ART regimens could save $300–380 million annually in drug costs across lowand middle-income countries accessing generic antiretroviral (ARV) drugs. The price of DTG varies significantly between countries, depending on licensing agreements and the availability of generic formulations. Ninety-two countries are eligible to procure generic DTG under a voluntary license agreement, while 39 additional countries can purchase generic versions due to the absence of patent restrictions. However, in highand upper-middle-income countries, non-generic DTG formulations are available at much higher costs, often exceeding $1,000 per person per year. Some lowand middle-income countries that adopted DTG early negotiated price reductions with the originator, achieving costs of $200–500 per person per year. For instance, the cost of DTG in Mexico is $2,200 per person per year, $500 in Brazil, and $1,600 in Belarus. In contrast, countries like Ukraine and Botswana have significantly lower costs at $72 and $272 per person per year, respectively. In countries where generic DTG is available, the cost of DTG-based ART is comparable to or lower than EFV-based ART. The first generic DTG single formulation was only recently commercialized, and triple fixed-dose combinations were expected to become available by late 2017 or early 2018. Generic DTG is substantially cheaper than protease inhibitor/ritonavir (PI/r)-based regimens, such as lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) at $223 per person per year, atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) at $197, and darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) at $908. However, in countries where generic DTG cannot be procured, the cost of PI/r regimens, while high, may still be lower than DTG. Modeling studies were conducted to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of three policy options in settings with elevated pre-treatment HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) to NNRTIs. These options included: (1) introducing a DTG-based regimen for all new first-line ART initiators, (2) implementing pre-treatment HIVDR testing to guide regimen selection, and (3) continuing with NNRTI-based regimens for all first-line ART starters. The modeling predicted that in sub-Saharan Africa, where the cost of DTG-based regimens is similar to EFV-based regimens, using DTG as the first-line treatment would be cost-effective and potentially cost-saving, regardless of the prevalence of pre-treatment HIVDR to NNRTIs. This is due to the superior properties of DTG, which benefit individuals even without drug-resistant HIV. The cost-effectiveness of PI/r-based regimens was not directly compared to DTG-based regimens in recent modeling studies, as PI/r regimens are more expensive in sub-Saharan Africa, and randomized trials have demonstrated the superiority of DTG as a first-line treatment. However, previous comparisons of PI/r regimens with NNRTI-based regimens suggested that PI/r regimens could be cost-effective when pre-treatment HIVDR to NNRTIs exceeded 15%, assuming a cost-effectiveness threshold of $2,000 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted. This threshold, however, is unlikely to be realistic in low-income settings. Surveys conducted among healthcare workers, ART program managers, and people living with HIV revealed varying levels of acceptance and challenges associated with transitioning to DTG-based regimens. Key challenges included the need for healthcare worker training, ensuring the availability of alternative regimens, and addressing cost and supply chain management issues. Despite these challenges, the majority of respondents supported the transition to DTG-based regimens, particularly in settings with high levels of pre-treatment HIVDR. In countries like Botswana and Brazil, national policies have already shifted to DTG-based first-line regimens, supported by cost-effectiveness studies and the drug's favorable safety and efficacy profile. These transitions were driven by concerns over rising pre-treatment HIVDR and the need for more effective and tolerable treatment options. While cost implications were considered, strategies such as optimizing the use of other ARV drugs and improving procurement efficiency helped mitigate the financial impact. Overall, the introduction of DTG-based regimens is expected to improve clinical outcomes, reduce costs, and enhance equity in HIV treatment, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. However, certain populations, such as pregnant women, individuals requiring concomitant tuberculosis treatment, and children, may require alternative regimens due to limited safety and efficacy data for DTG in these groups.
